1531–1547 · 16th century

The Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and imperial cities of the Holy Roman Empire, founded at Schmalkalden in 1531 and led by Philip of Hesse and John Frederick of Saxony. It resisted Emperor Charles V's efforts to restore Catholic unity until its defeat in the Schmalkaldic War, at Mühlberg in 1547. Members such as Constance and Lingen were then punished with loss of status or land.
## Origins
The League was officially established on 27 February 1531 as a defensive religious alliance: its members pledged to defend each other if Emperor Charles V attacked their territories. At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession. # Schmalkaldic League

Schmalkaldic League, during the Reformation, a defensive alliance formed by Protestant territories of the Holy Roman Empire to defend themselves collectively against any attempt to enforce the recess of the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, which gave the Protestant territories a deadline by which to return to Catholic practices. Established in February 1531 at Schmalkalden, Germany, the league was led by Landgrave Philip the Magnanimous of Hesse and John Frederick I of Saxony. Among its other original members were Brunswick, Anhalt, and the cities of Mansfeld, Magdeburg, Bremen, Strassburg, and Ulm. The league had a timeline of six years but was regularly extended.

Fearing that the league would ally itself with his enemy, Francis I of France, the emperor Charles V was forced to grant it de facto recognition until 1544, when he made peace with Francis. IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .infobox .IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .navbox .IPA-label-small{font-size:100%}English: /ʃmɔːlˈkɔːldɪk/; German: Schmalkaldischer Bund; Medieval Latin: Foedus Smalcaldicum or Liga Smalcaldica) was a military alliance of Lutheran principalities and cities within the Holy Roman Empire during the mid-16th century. Although created for religious motives soon after the start of the Reformation, its members later came to have the intention that the League would replace the Holy Roman Empire as their focus of political allegiance.[2]

At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession.[5]

The formation of the Schmalkaldic League in 1531 and the threatening attitude of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, who, in April 1532, assumed the offensive with an army of 300,000 men, caused Ferdinand of Austria to grant the religious peace.

Since the time of the Peasants’ War, the evangelical princes and city regimes had talked about forming a defensive military league to protect themselves, their lands, and their cities in the event that the Edict of Worms (which forbade their religion) were imposed on them by force. Still, the intra-evangelical doctrinal dispute prevented the formation of an alliance for another eighteen months. On December 23, 1535, nearly five years later, twenty-three estates approved the constitution of the Schmalkaldic League (B). Smalcald League

The Smalcald League (also called the Schmalkaldic League) was a defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and cities in the Holy Roman Empire. It took shape at Schmalkalden in the winter of 1530–1531, after the Diet of Augsburg left the Protestant estates facing the threat of imperial force. For about fifteen years it protected the spread of the Reformation in Germany, and it set agreement with the Augsburg Confession as a condition of membership. Internal weakness, the shifting loyalty of Maurice of Saxony, and Emperor Charles V's freedom from foreign wars brought its defeat in the Smalcald War (1546–1547). The Lutheran territories nevertheless won legal recognition in the Peace of Augsburg (1555).

Name and setting

The league took its name from Schmalkalden (older English spelling Smalcald), a small town in the Thuringian Forest in central Germany. At the time it was under the lordship of Hesse. It lay conveniently between the lands of the two leading Protestant rulers, the elector of Saxony and the landgrave of Hesse, and their representatives met there repeatedly during the 1530s. The same town gave its name to the Smalcald Articles , the statement of faith that Martin Luther prepared for one of the league's meetings.

1. History
2. Reformation and Catholic Reform

1531–1555

On 27 February 1531 Protestant princes and cities formed the Schmalkaldic League to defend against the emperor. The Peace of Nuremberg in 1532 temporarily halted persecution.

Luther died on 18 February 1546. After his death Charles V crushed the League in the Schmalkaldic War, at the Battle of Mühlberg on 24 April 1547. He imposed on the Protestants first the Augsburg and then the milder Leipzig Interim. This provoked bitter adiaphoristic and other disputes within Lutheranism.

A revolt of Protestant princes led by Maurice of Saxony forced the emperor into the Peace of Passau. In September 1555 the Peace of Augsburg established the principle "cuius regio, eius religio" (whose realm, his religion). It recognized only Catholicism and Lutheranism and left the Reformed outside the law. Charles V soon abdicated.

## Key points

- Founding of the Schmalkaldic League (27 February 1531)
- Defeat of the League at Mühlberg (24 April 1547)
- The Augsburg and Leipzig Interims and the adiaphorist controversy
- The Peace of Augsburg (September 1555): "whose realm, his religion"
- Kusukawa: after Charles V’s harsh reaction the Protestant princes signed the Augsburg Confession at Schmalkalden (30 Dec. 1530), and the league was formally constituted in February 1531. The **Battle of Mühlberg** was a decisive engagement of the Schmalkaldic War, fought on 24 April 1547 near Mühlberg in Saxony, in which the imperial army under Holy Roman Emperor Charles V routed the Protestant forces of the Schmalkaldic League commanded by Elector John Frederick I of Saxony.

The imperial coalition, bolstered by the alliance of Saxon Duke Maurice—who had defected from the Protestant cause—comprised approximately 10,000 to 20,000 troops, including veteran Spanish tercios, and surprised the League's army of comparable size across the Elbe River. The battle resulted in heavy Protestant losses, estimated at 2,000 to 3,000 dead or wounded alongside over 1,000 prisoners, while imperial casualties numbered fewer than 100; John Frederick was captured shortly after, and Landgrave Philip I of Hesse surrendered soon thereafter.

## Abstract

Since the time of the Peasants’ War, the evangelical princes and city regimes had talked about forming a defensive military league to protect themselves, their lands, and their cities in the event that the Edict of Worms (which forbade their religion) were imposed on them by force. Early efforts failed because the leading southern cities refused to enter into an alliance with the princes, and, more importantly, because the evangelical party was split between the followers of Luther, on the one hand, and Zwingli, on the other, over the meaning of the Lord’s Supper (Eucharist). The Schmalkaldic League was a German Protestant military federation based on an agreement made at Schmalkalden in Thuringia in December 1530 and ratified in February 1531. The presidency of the league alternated between the elector and the landgrave.

The league, originally formed for six years, ratified a fixed constitution at Schmalkalden on 23 December 1535, which was almost immediately revised in October 1536 because of the growth in league membership. The cities of Esslingen, Brunswick, Goslar, Einbeck, and Göttingen all joined the league between 1531 and 1535. In 1535 the dukes of Pomerania and Württemberg, the count of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, two princes of Anhalt-Dessau, and the cities of Frankfurt am Main, Kempten, Hamburg, and Hannover all joined the league. Under the new constitution the league was divided into two "circles": a northern, "Saxon" circle and a southern, "upper German" circle.

Fearing that the league would ally itself with his enemy, Francis I of France, the emperor Charles V was forced to grant it de facto recognition until 1544, when he made peace with Francis. He then began military operations against the league in 1546—the War of Schmalkald—and effectively defeated it in 1547.

The Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and imperial cities of the Holy Roman Empire, founded at Schmalkalden in 1531 and led by Philip of Hesse and John Frederick of Saxony. It resisted Emperor Charles V's efforts to restore Catholic unity until its defeat in the Schmalkaldic War, at Mühlberg in 1547. Members such as Constance and Lingen were then punished with loss of status or land. Three years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism official status in the Holy Roman Empire and let princes choose the religion of their domains, by the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.

The Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance formed in 1531 among Protestant princes and cities in the Holy Roman Empire during the Reformation. It emerged in response to the growing pressures from Catholic powers, particularly the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, who sought to enforce Catholicism and suppress Lutheranism following earlier treaties like the Edict of Worms.
When Charles solemnly demanded that all Protestants conform to the Catholic Church by April 15, 1531, the Diet broke up and Protestant leaders began preparing for armed resistance. At Schmalkald, on February 27, 1531, Protestant leaders formed a Protestant League, with Philip the Magnanimous as its unofficial head.
Over time, it achieved notable successes, including the establishment of the Peace of Augsburg in 1555, which allowed German princes to choose the official religion of their territories, thereby legitimizing Lutheranism alongside Catholicism. Despite internal divisions and challenges, the Schmalkaldic League was crucial in the consolidation of Protestantism in Northern Europe and the shaping of religious and political landscapes during that era.
